title: A Rock and China's Three-Sea Problem
gist: Shuxian Luo argues that a July dispute over Sino-Russian drills near Japan's tiny Okinotori feature is one node in a broader, increasingly coherent Chinese pattern — pairing lawfare with intensified drills and patrols — for managing simultaneous pressure across the East China Sea, South China Sea, and Taiwan Strait as Japan, the Philippines, and Taiwan draw closer together, and that Washington's selective silence on Okinotori (versus its vocal stance on the 2016 South China Sea ruling elsewhere) undercuts U.S. credibility on a rules-based maritime order.

themes.theme: The Okinotori dispute and its legal weakness

insights.claim: Okinotori is a feature with a total land size of less than 10 square meters at high tide, yet it is the entire legal basis on which Japan claims a 150,000-square-mile exclusive economic zone — an area nearly the size of Japan itself — located more than 1,000 miles south of Tokyo.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale mismatch driving the legal dispute (10 sq meters generating a 150,000 sq mile EEZ), useful shorthand for assessing how exposed Japan's maritime claim is to legal challenge.

insights.claim: The 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling, which found many Spratly features China claims as islands are merely rocks under UNCLOS, directly and 'ironically' undermines Japan's own claim that Okinotori is an island, since Okinotori cannot pass the ruling's test of sustaining human habitation or economic life in its natural form.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural legal trap for Japan: the same 2016 ruling Tokyo champions against China's South China Sea claims logically invalidates Japan's own Okinotori EEZ claim — a consistency problem investors in Japan-China maritime-risk scenarios should track.

insights.claim: By 2016, Japan had spent over $600 million protecting Okinotori from erosion and building an observatory to monitor passing ships, yet the feature in its natural form has not sustained human habitation or economic activity of its own, as UNCLOS Article 121 requires for island status.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Quantifies Japan's sunk-cost exposure ($600M+) in defending a legally weak maritime claim — relevant to assessing Tokyo's incentive to keep the claim alive despite its shaky legal footing.

insights.claim: China, South Korea, and Taiwan all reject Okinotori's status as an island (China first objected in 2004, with China and South Korea filing formal notes verbales to the U.N. Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf since 2009), but none of the three challenges Japan's sovereignty over the feature itself — only its legal status and the maritime zones that status generates.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Clarifies the dispute is narrowly legal/zonal, not a sovereignty contest, which bounds the realistic escalation risk around Okinotori itself even as it feeds broader regional tension.
insights.locator: What Is Disputed and What Is Not

insights.claim: Because Japan's own EEZ claim around Okinotori rests on shaky legal ground, Tokyo protested the July Sino-Russian live-fire drills there only on safety grounds and did not call them unlawful — an omission that let Beijing insist the drills were conducted on the 'high seas' and 'fully consistent with international law.'
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Shows China exploiting Japan's own legal vulnerability in real time to legitimize military activity near Japan — a template for how Beijing may handle future incursions near other Japanese-claimed maritime features.

insights.claim: China's show of force at Okinotori was more than pushback against Japan's 10th-anniversary statement on the 2016 arbitration ruling — it came as a hardened response to Japan's deepening security partnership with the Philippines, including a 2025 Reciprocal Access Agreement and a 2026 Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Identifies two specific, named 2025-2026 Japan-Philippines defense agreements (Reciprocal Access, Acquisition and Cross-Servicing) as the deeper trigger behind China's Okinotori response — concrete alliance-deepening milestones to track for further Chinese counter-moves.

insights.claim: Japan's Official Development Assistance financed maritime capacity-building for the Philippines, including the transfer of 10 coast guard patrol ships, and Japan's 2022 creation of the Official Security Assistance program was dedicated to strengthening partners' capabilities to 'prevent unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force.'
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified data point (10 patrol ships transferred) on Japan's material investment in Philippine maritime capacity — relevant to tracking Japan's expanding security-assistance footprint in Southeast Asia.

insights.claim: China's exercises at Okinotori were also likely a warning over Japan's maritime boundary delimitation talks with the Philippines, launched in May 2026 and covering waters east of Taiwan, which Beijing denounces as encroaching on Chinese maritime rights.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, dated (May 2026) trilateral boundary-delimitation process as a fresh flashpoint likely to draw further Chinese coercive responses.
insights.locator: The exercises were likely also intended as a warning

insights.claim: Since 2025, Japan and the Philippines have floated a 'one-theater' concept treating the East and South China Seas as a single operational space, and leaders of both countries have suggested their nations would likely be drawn into any fight over Taiwan — remarks that alarmed Beijing.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: A named strategic concept ('one-theater') signaling Japan-Philippines military coordination is moving toward explicit multi-front linkage — a key structural shift raising the odds that a Taiwan contingency draws in simultaneous East and South China Sea fronts.
insights.locator: Since 2025, the Philippines and Japan have floated

insights.claim: Chinese military strategists, per canonical works like Science of Military Strategy, have long warned of a 'three-sea linkage' or 'chain reaction' in which rival claimants coordinate with each other and the U.S. to open pressure or conflict on multiple fronts while China must concentrate on Taiwan — their doctrinal answer is to concentrate on the primary direction (Taiwan) while holding the line on secondary fronts.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Reveals China's own doctrinal playbook for a multi-front East China Sea/South China Sea/Taiwan Strait crisis — a framework for forecasting where China would concentrate force versus merely hold the line in a real Taiwan contingency.
insights.locator: This is precisely the security landscape China's strategists

insights.claim: China pairs legal instruments with expanded physical presence at each point of contention on a discernible, theater-tailored pattern: at Okinotori, drills plus the Article 121 legal test; at Scarborough Shoal, joint military-coast guard drills plus new nature-reserve administration rules; east of Taiwan, coast guard patrols plus invocation of the One China principle to act on Taipei's behalf.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern-recognition framework: each new China-claimant friction point should be expected to combine a legal/administrative move with a matched military/coast-guard escalation, useful for anticipating China's next moves in ongoing disputes.
insights.locator: On the Japan front, Beijing coupled the exercises

insights.claim: Tensions in the East China Sea have escalated since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's 2025 remarks that a Taiwan emergency could threaten Japan's survival, building on a trajectory that includes China firing five ballistic missiles into Japan's exclusive economic zone in 2022 following Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan visit.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Traces the East China Sea escalation timeline from a 2022 missile incident to a named 2025 statement by Japan's PM explicitly linking Taiwan security to Japan's own survival — a rhetorical escalation marker for gauging how tightly Japan now ties itself to a Taiwan contingency.
insights.quote: a Taiwan emergency could threaten Japan's survival
insights.locator: In the East China Sea, tensions have been escalating

insights.claim: Taiwan's Lai Ching-te government has taken a tougher line toward Beijing's pressure campaign than his predecessor Tsai Ing-wen, and Beijing regards Lai as a committed pro-independence figure, contributing to steadily rising tension across the Taiwan Strait since his 2024 inauguration.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Confirms Lai's administration is assessed (by this author) as more confrontational toward Beijing than its predecessor, a factor sustaining elevated cross-Strait tension and Taiwan-risk premia.
insights.locator: across the Taiwan Strait, tensions have increased steadily

insights.claim: Excluded from the Japan-Philippines maritime boundary talks and choosing not to press its own overlapping claims, Taiwan's Lai government left a vacuum that Beijing stepped into, invoking its One China principle to assert rights on Taiwan's behalf and sending coast guard vessels to patrol waters east of Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Documents a live mechanism by which Beijing expands its coast-guard presence east of Taiwan under legal pretext — a specific, trackable pattern of gray-zone pressure that could establish a 'new normal' presence with implications for Taiwan Strait shipping and security risk.

insights.claim: Taiwan's dilemma is a strategic trade-off, not legal inconsistency: aligning with Tokyo and Manila against Chinese pressure may require Taipei to acquiesce to a Japanese EEZ around Okinotori and a Japan-Philippines delimitation reached without Taiwan at the table, in exchange for partnerships it badly needs — and it remains unclear whether Taipei can defend this trade-off domestically.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Flags a potential domestic-political friction point in Taiwan (fisheries/sovereignty concessions for security partnerships) that could complicate the Japan-Philippines-Taiwan alignment Beijing fears most.
insights.locator: For Taiwan, the dilemma is a strategic trade-off

insights.claim: The United States has long championed the 2016 arbitration ruling against China's expansive South China Sea claims but has stayed conspicuously silent on Okinotori, whose Japanese EEZ claim rests on the same legal reasoning the ruling would invalidate — a selective consistency the author says lets Beijing cast the U.S.-backed rules-based order as 'rules for others, not for the United States or its friends.'
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: A reputational-risk factor for U.S. alliance credibility in the Indo-Pacific: selective legal consistency on Okinotori feeds a Chinese narrative that undermines the broader rules-based order the U.S. relies on to rally third-party support against Beijing's South China Sea claims.
insights.quote: rules for others, not for the United States or its friends
insights.locator: Deliberate ambiguity, however, can play into Beijing's hand

insights.claim: The author recommends the U.S. take the position that the 2016 ruling's Article 121 interpretation applies universally to features claimed by friend and foe alike, without declaring any specific feature (including Okinotori) a rock — a stance she argues would cost only 'manageable friction' with Japan while denying Beijing its favorite rhetorical double-standard argument.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: A specific, low-cost policy recommendation for Washington to strengthen its Indo-Pacific legal credibility without damaging the Japan alliance — worth watching for whether the U.S. actually adopts this more consistent posture.
insights.locator: The cost of consistency is manageable friction with an ally

insights.claim: Legal consistency on maritime-feature status could also force the United States to reconsider its own claims to expansive zones around remote uninhabited islets such as Howland and Baker Islands, a cost the author notes as a reason some defend current U.S. selectivity.
insights.speaker: Shuxian Luo
insights.so_what: Identifies a direct blowback risk to the U.S.'s own remote-island EEZ claims (Howland, Baker Islands) if it pushes full legal consistency on the island-vs-rock question — a factor likely to keep U.S. policy ambiguous despite the author's recommendation.
insights.locator: legal consistency might even force the United States
